video.title: The Lazy Way to Launch Your Online Business

summary: George McConnell demonstrates how to list personalised print-on-demand pet pillows and suncatchers, using Etsy listings to estimate demand and InkJoy to customise and fulfil products. He shows supplier options, competitor prices, sales estimates, AI-generated advertising and product infographics, and store integrations. He also briefly mentions a future swimsuit line, glass ornaments and other apparel and accessory products. His main takeaway is to validate demand, make product listings visually clear and use a supplier that handles production and shipping.

speakers.name: George McConnell
speakers.description: Solo host; promotes his E365 community and InkJoy links.

ideas.name: Personalised pet-shaped pillows
ideas.one_liner: Sell customers a custom pillow made from a photo of their pet, fulfilled through a print-on-demand supplier.
ideas.business_model: Per-item sales through a marketplace or an online store; print-on-demand fulfilment.
ideas.customer: Online shoppers buying personalised pet products or gifts. The host says many buyers of animal-related products on Etsy are women.
ideas.problem: Not stated. The host says people love their pets and spend money on them.
ideas.offer: A pillow customised from a customer's pet photo, with several shapes and sizes. InkJoy removes the photo background. A voice-recording version is also shown.

pricing.model: Per-item retail sale, with separate product and shipping charges; supplier prices are also shown.

price_points.label: InkJoy price; exact size or variant is unclear
Shipping charged on the observed retail listing

pricing.notes: The host compares supplier and retail prices but does not account for all fees or costs when discussing profit.

acquisition_channels.details: The host checks Etsy and Amazon listings to validate demand and suggests Etsy or Amazon as places to sell.
The host suggests selling through a Shopify or WooCommerce website, where customers can upload their own photo.
The host points to a competitor's Meta ads and suggests using Facebook ads for a store.

ideas.delivery: The seller creates the listing and connects it to InkJoy. Customers can upload a photo through a connected Shopify store; the host says Etsy can also support the process but does not explain the exact workflow. InkJoy removes the background, makes the pillow and fulfils the order. The host shows a version with a voice recording.
unit_economics_claims: The host reports third-party pillow listings with 456 sales in six months and 236 in one month.
He cites Amazon listings displaying 100, 400, 50 and 200 sold.
He shows a $19 retail price for a 12-inch pillow and a $26 retail price plus $7 shipping for a 15-inch pillow.
He shows InkJoy prices of $4 and $6.60, with shipping prices of $5.76 and $7; the exact variant mapping for the $4 price is unclear.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; the host shows supplier product and shipping prices but gives no launch budget.

acquisition.how: Marketplace listings and paid social can bring inbound orders; AI can help make ad creative. Ad spend, targeting and creative still need human review. The host does not propose direct outreach.

onboarding.how: A connected Shopify flow can let customers upload their photo themselves. A person would still need to handle exceptions and check unclear customer files.

delivery.how: InkJoy handles background removal, production and fulfilment. A person may still need to review proofs, quality problems or delivery exceptions.

billing.how: The host proposes sales through Etsy, Shopify or WooCommerce integrations, where checkout can be handled by the platform; exceptions and reconciliation may need review.

support.how: Routine order updates could be automated, but questions about personal photos, product quality, shipping delays and refunds are likely to need human review.

uk_applicability.notes: The product and online-store model can work in the UK. A seller would need to localise prices and shipping and account for UK tax and consumer requirements.

risks: The host uses third-party sales estimates and visible marketplace counts as demand signals; these do not establish the seller's likely sales or profit.
The host does not provide a full margin calculation including marketplace and payment fees, advertising, refunds or other costs.
The AI-generated ad script mispronounces the pet's name, illustrating the need to check generated creative.
The host calls the generated ad a review, but does not establish that it is a real customer's testimonial. Presenting fabricated endorsements as real could mislead buyers.
Customers provide pet photos, so the store needs a clear process for handling and deleting customer images.

ideas.name: Personalised pet suncatchers
ideas.one_liner: Sell a custom suncatcher printed with a customer's pet photo as a personalised home or gift product.
ideas.business_model: Per-item sales through a marketplace or online store; print-on-demand fulfilment.
ideas.customer: Online shoppers who want a personalised pet item or gift. The host says people love their pets and buy pet-related products.
ideas.problem: Not stated. The host presents the product as a visually appealing way to display a pet image.
ideas.offer: A suncatcher customised with a pet photo. InkJoy removes the photo background; the product comes in different colours, is printed on one side, and includes a box and suction cup.

pricing.model: Per-item retail sale; print-on-demand supplier cost for this product is not stated.
pricing.notes: The $50 price is from a competing listing shown by the host.

acquisition_channels.details: The host researches Etsy listings and suggests Etsy as a possible sales channel.
The host says the product can be pushed to a connected store; Shopify and WooCommerce are discussed as store options.
The host points to a competitor's Meta ads and suggests Facebook ads for an independent store.

ideas.delivery: The seller creates the listing and submits the customer's pet photo through InkJoy. InkJoy removes the background, prints the suncatcher and fulfils the order. The host says the design can be pushed to a connected store.
unit_economics_claims: The host reports third-party Etsy suncatcher listings with 880 sales in seven months, 308 in one month, 155 in four months, and 1,000 in 25 months.
He shows a competing 8-inch suncatcher listed at $50.
The host says his InkJoy order arrived in seven business days; a competing listing showed an estimated delivery about 25 days away.

acquisition.how: Marketplace listings and paid social can bring inbound orders. The host demonstrates AI-assisted infographics, but a person should review images and advertising.

onboarding.how: The store can collect the chosen photo and colour through its order flow. Unclear uploads or custom requests may need human handling.

delivery.how: InkJoy removes the background and fulfils the physical product. A person may still need to review quality and delivery exceptions.

billing.how: The host discusses connected ecommerce platforms and marketplace sales; routine checkout can run through those platforms, with human review for exceptions.

support.how: Routine updates could be automated, but product, photo, quality, shipping and refund questions may need human judgement.

uk_applicability.notes: The product and online-sales model can work in the UK. Localise currency and shipping, and account for UK tax and consumer requirements.

risks: The host relies on competitor sales estimates and listing prices; they do not establish the seller's own demand or margins.
The host does not state the supplier cost, so the $50 listing price alone does not show profit.
Shipping times can vary; the host's seven-business-day order and the competing listing's estimated 25-day delivery are individual examples.

tactics.name: Validate product demand before listing
steps: Search Etsy for comparable products and inspect their sales history.
Use Everbee to estimate recent sales for individual listings.
Cross-check demand on Amazon by looking at the sold counts shown on listings.
Treat these figures as demand signals, not as proof of your own likely sales.

quote.text: Now, before you sell or launch any product, you always need to make sure and validate that it actually does sell.
quote.speaker: George McConnell

tactics.name: Use listing variants and reviews to select a product size
steps: Review the sizes buyers selected in the competitor listing's reviews.
Look for a size that appears more often; the host identifies 15 inches as the apparent top seller.
Compare that size's retail price with the supplier product and shipping prices.

quote.text: So 15 seems like it is really the top seller. So I come up here, go to the 15 in, and as you can see right there, it's $26.
quote.speaker: George McConnell

tactics.name: Create AI-assisted product advertising
steps: Provide ChatGPT with a reference image and a description of the product.
Specify the desired model, pose and audience, and include negative prompts for unwanted appearance details.
Use Higgsfield with a reference, spoken script, behaviour prompt and voice settings to create a short video.
Review the output before using it; the host's example mispronounces the pet's name.

quote.text: I said, "Hey, I want a handsome athletic man in his late 20s holding a custom pet shape pillow."
quote.speaker: George McConnell

tactics.name: Make the product listing visually informative
steps: Create an infographic showing the uploaded photo, customised product, name and colour choices.
Show what arrives in the box and how the product hangs.
Explain details such as the one-sided print so buyers know what to expect.
Keep the visuals easy to scan instead of filling the image with text.

quote.text: So, jumping in the ChatGPT, you can see I've already made a couple here, all right?
